name: Kuuk Thaayorre
confidence_why: Gaby's 2006 grammar (revised 2017) places primary stress on the first syllable of the lexical head and cites Alpher 1972 for the same root-initial pattern, but Hall's 1968 phonology and 1972 grammar of the same Edward River community call stress phonemic and report suffixes often accented more strongly than the root, a claim Gaby checked against her own recordings and rejected.

catalog_quote: Primary stress in Kuuk Thaayorre is allocated to the first syllable of the lexical head (cf. Alpher’s 1972:71 similar claim that stress falls on the root-initial syllable in both Kuuk Thaayorre and Yir Yoront). Since Kuuk Thaayorre is a predominantly suffixing language, the initial syllable of the lexical head usually but not always corresponds to the first syllable of the phonological word. Examples of nonalignment, where the lexical head is not the word-initial morpheme, are compounds and two enclitics. It is generally the second root of a compound that receives primary stress (e.g. /puŋk+pá:nt/ ‘kneecap [lit. knee+head]’, mè:ɻ+kun+wá:r ‘pitiful [lit. eye+guts+bad]’). The enclitics /=(k)a:k/ ‘proprietive’ and /=(k)a:ɻ / ‘privative’ are unusual both in their tendency to attract primary stress and in the fact that they contain long vowels (these two features being clearly related). .…

Every sentence in the repo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the lexical root (head), which in this suffixing language is normally the word-initial syllable; only compounds (second root stressed) and the two long-vowelled enclitics =(k)a:k 'proprietive' and =(k)a:r 'privative' (which attract primary stress) break the word-initial alignment. Long vowels occur only in stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: For most words, secondary stress falls on every second syllable after the initial stressed one (e.g. /máŋkwarkàntɻ/); when a stress-attracting enclitic carries primary stress the word-initial syllable takes secondary stress with intervening syllables unstressed (/jì:ramokunká:k/). Final syllables of odd-syllabled words vary: /máŋk.war.kànt/ has final secondary stress, /ŋát̪n-m(a)n/ does not, depending on the syllable's phonotactic shape, root vs suffix status, and position in the intonational phrase.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds stress the second root (/puŋk+pá:nt/ 'kneecap', mè:ɻ+kun+wá:r 'pitiful'); enclitics =(k)a:k PROP and =(k)a:ɻ PRIV attract primary stress; stress may shift for discursive/contrastive effect in spontaneous speech (/irkuw/ 'to the west' once pronounced i:r-kúw); Koko Mincena is noted as a rare penultimate-stress word (ch. 1). Gaby explicitly contradicts Hall (1968:61, 151), who reported second-morpheme/suffix stress ([pòkhón], /ŋàtún/); in her data /pókon/ and /ngát̪un/ are initially stressed (she speculates Hall's consultants stressed contrastive suffixes in elicitation).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root + suffixes + enclitics), based on elicited and narrative/conversational recordings 2002-2005; Gaby flags the suprasegmental description as preliminary ('warrants much deeper investigation') and refers readers to Hall 1968 for fuller exemplification. Noun phrases carry a single primary stress peak (ch. 6).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Kuuk Thaayorre as spoken at Pormpuraaw (Edward River), the same variety Glottolog lists as thay1249 (ISO thd); Hall's 1968/1972 theses describe the same Edward River community a generation earlier. No dialect issue.

Reading: the sentence says only that stress is phonemic (contrastive) and gives no placement…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog and Gaby 2006 record fixed initial stress (first syllable of the lexical head). Hall's abstract instead calls stress phonemic, i.e. contrastive, a different type. Gaby 2006:67 explicitly rejects Hall's 1968 suffix-stress observations ('These findings stand contrary to Hall's (1968:61) observations..') and speculates (fn. 48) that Hall's consultants stressed contrastive suffixes in elicitation. Confidence low: abstract-level statement only.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The abstract asserts only that stress is phonemic (contrastive) in Thaayorre; it gives no placement rule. Read together with Hall's 1968 observations as quoted by Gaby 2006:67 (suffixes and second morphemes often carry stronger accent than the root-initial syllable), Hall treats stress as a distinctive, not positionally fixed, feature. The claim cannot be checked against the thesis body.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Hall works describe the Thaayorre of the Edward River mission (now Pormpuraaw), the same variety as Gaby 2006 and thay1249. Hall 1968 additionally contains material on Wik Mungkan, Uw Olkola, Yir Yoront, Kugu Muminh, Wik Ngatharr and Kugu Nganhcara (per the UQ record note), so its stress remarks would need checking for which language they concern; the pages Gaby quotes (61, 151) concern Thaayorre.

new_statements.quote: p. 64: "Stress in the Ta:yor word is non-phonemic and always morpheme-initial: e.g. ['wɛ.lɛ] 'bailer-shell' ['ta.wat] 'dish'. Nouns preceded by a noun-classifier are neither joined nor hyphenated in this work. Each comprises normally a single morpheme and has its own predictable word-initial stress which affects the aspiration of stops [...] Words comprising two or more morphemes, such as a noun + suffix, have an accent on the initial syllable of each half". p. 151: "But operative suffixes frequently receive greater stress than initial syllables of the root-morpheme: e.g. /'natn/ 'my'; cf. /'ŋa"t-un/ 'to me'. [...] Ta:yor is an intonation language like English, and does not have lexical tone to distinguish contrasts of meaning." (fn. 4: "Phrase stress is independent of morpheme-initial stress.")

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (initial: initial stress) and with Gaby 2006 section 2.8.1 that stress is predictable and initial, and states explicitly that it is non-phonemic and that the language has no lexical tone. Adds the morpheme as the stress domain (an accent on the first syllable of every morpheme) and the stop-aspiration correlate. One point of tension with Gaby 2006's formulation (primary stress on the first syllable of the lexical head): Hall reports that in polymorphemic words the suffix-initial accent is frequently STRONGER than the root-initial one (pp. 61, 151) -- Gaby 2006:67 herself quotes these two Hall passages. This concerns relative prominence among morpheme-initial a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-phonemic (predictable) and falls on the first syllable of each morpheme; a monomorphemic word therefore has word-initial stress (correlated with aspirated, voiceless fortis initial stops). In words of two or more morphemes each morpheme-initial syllable carries an accent, the word-initial one diminishing to medium intensity (abstract p. 4), and the second morpheme / 'operative' suffix may compete with and even receive a stronger accent than the root-initial syllable (pp. 61, 151); recurring directional particles do not attract this accent, primary stress staying word-initial (p. 62). No lexical tone; pitch is intonational; phrase stress is independent of morpheme-initial stress and can weaken it (p. 150, 204: 'Strong or medium stress morpheme-initially, weak elsewhere').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Each non-initial morpheme carries its own morpheme-initial accent ('an accent on the initial syllable of each half', p. 64; 'one medium and one loud', p. 183 area); in polymorphemic words the word-initial stress diminishes to medium and the suffix-initial accent is frequently the stronger one (pp. 4, 61, 151). Three degrees of loudness are distinguished (p. 151).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) In two-morpheme words the second morpheme 'tends to compete with the first and receives a stronger accent' (p. 61), 'operative suffixes frequently receive greater stress than initial syllables of the root-morpheme' (p. 151); (2) after word-initial long vowels with a following recurring directional particle, 'primary stress remains word-initial' (p. 62); (3) a reduplicated CV- prefix takes the stress and the original initial becomes unstressed (p. 65); (4) lexical stress may disappear in connected speech when a focused sentence-initial word is heavily stressed (p. 24), and utterance stress-rhythm may weaken morpheme-initial stress (p. 150); (5) vowel-initial words may take a dialectal prothetic /ŋ-/ 'as if initial vowels were inadequate to bear the common morpheme-initial stress' (p. 4).
new_statements.identity_note: Hall 1968 describes Ta:yor / Thaayorr as spoken at Edward River (now Pormpuraaw), west coast of Cape York Peninsula, principal phonology informant Lawrence Foot; this is the same community and variety as Gaby 2006's Kuuk Thaayorre (thay1249 / ISO thd). Hall notes minor dialectal variation (e.g. prothetic /ŋ-/ on vowel-initial words) but describes a single variety.

readall_conflicts: Hall (1968, 1972) versus Gaby (2006): Hall's 1972 abstract states that Thaayorre has "phonemic stress", and his 1968 phonology (as quoted by Gaby 2006:67) reports that second morphemes and operative suffixes often receive a stronger accent than the root-initial syllable ([pòkhón] 'nothing', /ŋàtún/ 'to me'). Gaby 2006:66-67 finds primary stress exclusively on the first syllable of the lexical head (/pókon/, /ngát̪un/), with secondary stress on alternate syllables, and states that her findings "stand contrary to Hall's (1968:61) observations", suggesting Hall's consultants stressed contrastive suffixes in elicitation. Neither Hall thesis body could be opened, so Hall's claims rest on his abstract and on Gaby's quotations; the fixed: initial syllable reading of the catalog stands on Gaby's opened text.
